content: The cabbage, scientifically known as Brassica oleracea Capitata Group, belongs to the family Brassicaceae (also called Cruciferae). It is a herbaceous, biennial, and dicotyledonous flowering plant characterized by its compact cluster of leaves. Cabbages cultivated in late autumn and early winter are referred to as coleworts. This vegetable is derived from a wild mustard plant native to the Mediterranean region. It was highly regarded by ancient Greeks and Romans, with Cato the Elder praising its medicinal properties and calling it the foremost of all vegetables. The English word cabbage originates from the Normanno-Picard term caboche, meaning head. The modern cabbage was developed through artificial selection to suppress internode length, resulting in its dense, compact form. The central core of the cabbage is known as the babchka. Cabbage is closely related to the turnip, and its sharp or bitter taste is attributed to the presence of glucosinolates. Uses The edible portion of the cabbage is the leafy head, specifically the spherical cluster of immature leaves, excluding the partially unfolded outer leaves. This cabbage head is consumed in various forms—raw, cooked, or preserved—and is a widely recognized leaf vegetable. Raw When consumed raw, cabbage is typically shredded or sliced into thin strips for use in salads, such as coleslaw. It can also serve as a substitute for iceberg lettuce in sandwiches. Raw cabbage is an excellent source of Vitamin C. Cooked Cabbage is frequently incorporated into soups and stews. It is a key ingredient in dishes like cabbage soup, which is popular in Central and Eastern Europe, as well as certain types of borscht. In Indian cuisine, cabbage is used in numerous recipes. Cooking cabbage, particularly by boiling, softens the leaves and releases sugars, which contribute to its characteristic aroma. However, boiled cabbage has been stigmatized in North America due to its strong odor during cooking and its association with flatulence. Despite this, boiled cabbage remains a valuable source of vitamins and dietary fiber when served as a side dish. Stuffed cabbage, a delicacy in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, involves softening the leaves through parboiling or freezing the entire head, then filling them with chopped meat and/or rice. Fermented and Preserved Cabbage serves as the base for fermented foods like German sauerkraut and Korean kimchi. To pickle cabbage, it is submerged in a brine of water and salt and left to ferment in a warm environment for several days. Historically, sauerkraut was prepared in large batches as a method of food preservation for the winter months. Cabbage can also be pickled in vinegar with various spices, either alone or combined with other vegetables. Korean baechu kimchi is typically sliced thicker than European sauerkraut and often includes ingredients like onions, chilies, minced garlic, and ginger. Medicinal Properties In European folk medicine, cabbage leaves have been used to treat acute inflammation. A paste made from raw cabbage can be applied to a cabbage leaf and wrapped around the affected area to alleviate discomfort. Some anecdotal evidence suggests that cabbage leaves may help relieve engorged breasts in breastfeeding women. Cabbage contains significant levels of glutamine, an amino acid with anti-inflammatory properties. Additionally, it is a source of indole-3-carbinol (I3C), a compound used as an adjuvant therapy for recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a condition caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11, which leads to growths in the airway and can be life-threatening. Varieties Cabbage varieties differ in shape and maturation time. Traditional varieties include Late Flat Dutch, Early Jersey Wakefield (a conical type), and Danish Ballhead (a late, round-headed variety). Savoy cabbage is distinguished by its round head and crinkled leaves. Red cabbage is a smaller, round-headed variety with dark red leaves. The Krautman variety is commonly used in commercial sauerkraut production. Cultivation Cabbage varieties are broadly categorized into early and late types. Early varieties mature in approximately 45 days, producing small heads that are best consumed fresh as they do not store well. Late varieties take about 87 days to mature and produce larger heads. Cabbage can be started indoors or sown directly into the soil. As a cool-season crop, it thrives in early and late plantings, avoiding the heat of summer. Effective pest control is crucial, especially in commercial production, where appearance is a key factor. Pesticides such as sevin and malathion are approved for use on cabbage. Caterpillars from the Pieridae family (commonly known as whites) are significant pests of brassicas, including cabbage. Historically, cabbage was a staple winter vegetable due to its excellent storage properties before the advent of refrigeration and long-distance produce shipping. China is the leading producer of cabbage, followed by India and the Russian Federation. Related Brassica oleracea Varieties The species Brassica oleracea includes several other cultivars beyond cabbage, each with distinct characteristics. These include broccoli (Italica Group), cauliflower (Botrytis Group), kale, collard greens, and spring greens (Acephala Group), kohlrabi (Gongylodes Group), Brussels sprouts (Gemmifera Group), Chinese kale or Chinese broccoli (Alboglabra Group), broccolini (Italica × Alboglabra Group), and broccoflower (Italica × Botrytis Group). Linguistic Associations During World War II, the term kraut (derived from cabbage) was used as a racial slur for Germans. In Hebrew, the phrase rosh kruv (cabbage head) is a colloquial term implying stupidity. In England during the late 1950s, French language textbooks introduced the phrase ma petite chou (my little cabbage) as a term of endearment from a man to a woman. This expression remains in use today, as illustrated in literature. Additionally, in England, cabbage is slang for cash, particularly paper money.
